- Sharing of profits is not conclusive. Section 6 directs that the real relation be seen from all facts. A lender whose interest varies with profits, a servant paid a share of profits, a deceased partner's widow or child receiving a share, and a seller of goodwill receiving a share of profits are not partners by that fact alone.
- Mutual agency is the true test (Cox v. Hickman).

questions.prompt: Explain the consequences of non-registration of a partnership firm.
questions.answer:
Section 69 disabilities:

- A partner of an unregistered firm cannot sue the firm or any partner to enforce a right arising from a contract or conferred by the Act.
- The firm cannot sue any third party to enforce a contract right.
- The firm cannot claim a set-off exceeding ₹100 or other proceeding to enforce a contract right.

Exceptions (section 69(3) and (4)): suit for dissolution, accounts or realisation of property of a dissolved firm; powers of an official assignee or receiver; firms with no place of business in the territories to which the Act extends; suits or set-offs up to ₹100 in value; rights not arising from contract (e.g. tort). Third parties can always sue the unregistered firm.

questions.prompt: Arun, Bina and Chetan are partners in a firm dealing in textiles. Without consulting the others, Arun (a) bought cloth worth ₹4,00,000 on credit for the firm and (b) compromised a claim of ₹3,00,000 that the firm had against a customer for ₹1,50,000. Is the firm bound? Decide with reasons.
questions.answer:
- Provision: section 18 - a partner is an agent of the firm. Section 19(1) - his act done to carry on, in the usual way, business of the kind carried on by the firm binds the firm. Section 19(2) - in the absence of usage or custom, implied authority does not extend to compromising or relinquishing any claim of the firm.
- (a) Buying cloth on credit is usual in a textile business; the firm is bound and all partners are jointly and severally liable (section 25).
- (b) Compromising a claim is outside implied authority under section 19(2)(c). Unless Bina and Chetan ratify or a trade custom allows it, the firm is not bound by the compromise.
- Conclusion: the firm is bound by (a) but not by (b).

questions.prompt: State the rights and liabilities of a minor admitted to the benefits of partnership, before and after attaining majority.
questions.answer:
Section 30.

- Before majority: may be admitted to benefits with consent of all partners; entitled to agreed share of profits and property; may inspect and copy accounts; may sue for accounts and share only when severing connection; liability limited to his share in the firm, no personal liability.
- On majority: within 6 months of attaining majority or of knowing of admission, whichever is later, he must give public notice of his election.
- If he elects to become a partner (or gives no notice): he is personally liable for all acts of the firm since his admission to benefits; his share is as agreed.
- If he elects not to become a partner: his rights and liabilities remain those of a minor up to the notice; his share is not liable for acts after the notice; he can sue partners for his share.

chapters.title: The Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
chapters.summary: Nature of an LLP, partners and designated partners, incorporation, liability, and comparison with a firm and a company.
chapters.lawAsOf: LLP Act, 2008 as amended by the LLP (Amendment) Act, 2021, up to 2026

lesson.heading: What an LLP is
lesson.body:
A **Limited Liability Partnership** is a **body corporate** formed and incorporated under the LLP Act, 2008. It is a **legal entity separate from its partners** with **perpetual succession** (section 3). It combines the flexibility of a partnership (internal affairs governed by an agreement) with the limited liability of a company.

Features:

- Separate legal entity: can own property, sue and be sued in its own name (section 14).
- Perpetual succession: change in partners does not affect its existence or liabilities.
- **Limited liability**: a partner is not personally liable for an obligation of the LLP solely because he is a partner (section 28). He is liable for his own wrongful acts.
- Mutual agency is limited: every partner is an agent of the **LLP**, but not of other partners (section 26).
- Governed by the **LLP agreement** (section 23); where there is none, or on matters it does not cover, the **First Schedule** applies.
- No maximum number of partners.
- The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 does **not** apply to an LLP (section 4).
- Name must end with 'Limited Liability Partnership' or 'LLP' (section 15).

lesson.heading: Partners and designated partners
lesson.body:
- **Partners** (section 5): any individual or body corporate may be a partner, subject to disqualifications (e.g. unsound mind, undischarged insolvent).
- **Minimum partners** (section 6): at least two. If the number falls below two and the LLP carries on business for **more than six months**, the person who is the only partner, and knows this, is **personally liable** for obligations incurred during that period.
- **Designated partners** (section 7): at least **two**, who must be **individuals**, and at least **one** must be **resident in India**. Where all partners are bodies corporate, each body corporate nominates an individual. Resident in India means a person who has stayed in India for not less than **120 days** during the financial year (after the 2021 amendment; earlier 182 days).
- Designated partners are responsible for compliance with the Act, filings and penalties (section 8).

Incorporation (sections 11-12): two or more persons associated for carrying on a lawful business with a view to profit subscribe their names to an **incorporation document** and file it with the **Registrar**. On registration, the Registrar issues a **certificate of incorporation**, which is conclusive evidence of incorporation.

lesson.heading: Liability, compliance and conversion
lesson.body:
- **Liability of LLP** (section 27): the LLP is liable for a partner's wrongful act or omission in the course of business or with its authority; not liable where the partner had no authority and the other party knew it.
- **Unlimited liability for fraud** (section 30): where an act is done to defraud creditors or for a fraudulent purpose, the LLP and the partners who acted with that intent have unlimited liability.
- **Contribution** (section 32): may be tangible, intangible, money, promissory notes, agreements to contribute cash or property, or services.
- **Books and filings** (section 34, 35): proper books, an annual **Statement of Account and Solvency**, and an **annual return** filed with the Registrar. Audit as prescribed (small LLPs below prescribed limits have lighter requirements).
- **Conversion into an LLP**: from a partnership firm (section 55, Second Schedule), a private company (section 56, Third Schedule), and an unlisted public company (section 57, Fourth Schedule).
- **Winding up**: voluntary or by the Tribunal (sections 63-64).

Comparison:

| Basis | Partnership firm | LLP | Company |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Governing Act | Partnership Act, 1932 | LLP Act, 2008 | Companies Act, 2013 |
| Legal entity | No | Yes, body corporate | Yes |
| Liability | Unlimited, joint and several | Limited to agreed contribution (except fraud) | Limited by shares / guarantee (unless unlimited company) |
| Registration | Optional | Compulsory | Compulsory |
| Partners / members | Minimum 2, maximum 50 (prescribed under the Companies Act, 2013) | Minimum 2, no maximum | Private: 2 to 200; public: minimum 7 |
| Mutual agency | Each partner agent of firm and others | Partner agent of LLP only | Members are not agents |
| Internal governance | Partnership deed | LLP agreement / First Schedule | MoA, AoA, Board |

lesson.heading: Exam tips and common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Write 'body corporate' and 'separate legal entity' in any LLP definition answer.
- Minimum two partners and minimum two designated partners are different rules. Designated partners must be individuals; partners may be bodies corporate.
- The six-month rule of section 6 creates **personal** liability only for the partner who knows he is the sole partner.
- Do not apply the Partnership Act to an LLP.
- A partner of an LLP is not liable for another partner's wrongful act, but the LLP is.

keyPoints: LLP: body corporate, separate legal entity, perpetual succession (section 3); Partnership Act does not apply (section 4).
Minimum 2 partners; below 2 for more than 6 months - sole partner who knows is personally liable (section 6).
Minimum 2 designated partners, individuals, at least 1 resident in India (120 days in the financial year) (section 7).
Partner is agent of the LLP, not of other partners (section 26); not personally liable solely as partner (section 28).
Fraud: unlimited liability of LLP and partners concerned (section 30).
Conversion: firm (section 55), private company (56), unlisted public company (57).

questions.prompt: An LLP is:
options: An association of persons without legal status
A body corporate and a legal entity separate from its partners
A registered partnership firm under the 1932 Act
A private company limited by guarantee
questions.explanation: Section 3 of the LLP Act, 2008: an LLP is a body corporate, separate from its partners, with perpetual succession.

questions.prompt: The minimum number of designated partners in an LLP is:
questions.explanation: Section 7: at least two designated partners who are individuals, at least one of whom is resident in India.

questions.prompt: For section 7 of the LLP Act, a 'resident in India' is a person who has stayed in India during the financial year for not less than:
questions.explanation: The LLP (Amendment) Act, 2021 reduced the requirement from 182 days to 120 days in the financial year.

questions.prompt: Where matters are not provided for in the LLP agreement, mutual rights and duties are governed by:
options: Table F of the Companies Act, 2013
The First Schedule to the LLP Act, 2008
questions.explanation: Section 23(4): in the absence of agreement on a matter, the First Schedule applies.

questions.prompt: Every partner of an LLP is, for the purpose of the business of the LLP, the agent of:
options: The LLP and all other partners
The LLP but not of other partners
Other partners but not the LLP
questions.explanation: Section 26. This is a key difference from a firm, where each partner is an agent of the firm and of the other partners.

questions.prompt: A private company is converted into an LLP under:
questions.explanation: Section 55 covers firms, section 56 private companies and section 57 unlisted public companies.

questions.prompt: Where an LLP carries on business with intent to defraud creditors, liability is:
options: Limited to the contribution of each partner
Unlimited for the LLP and the partners who acted with that intent
questions.explanation: Section 30: the LLP and the partners who acted with intent to defraud have unlimited liability for the debts and obligations concerned.

questions.prompt: A body corporate can be a partner of an LLP but cannot itself be a designated partner.
questions.explanation: Section 5 allows a body corporate as partner. Section 7 requires designated partners to be individuals; a body corporate partner nominates an individual to act as designated partner.

questions.prompt: The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 applies to an LLP for matters not covered by the LLP agreement.
questions.explanation: Section 4 of the LLP Act excludes the Partnership Act. The First Schedule to the LLP Act fills gaps.

questions.prompt: Which statements about an LLP are correct?
options: There is no maximum limit on the number of partners
It can own property in its own name
questions.explanation: An LLP comes into existence only on registration (section 12), so registration is compulsory. The rest are correct.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: The document filed with the Registrar to incorporate an LLP is called the ___ document.
questions.explanation: Section 11: two or more persons subscribe their names to an incorporation document and file it with the Registrar.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between an LLP and a partnership firm.
questions.answer:
| Basis | LLP | Partnership firm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Act | LLP Act, 2008 | Indian Partnership Act, 1932 |
| Legal status | Body corporate, separate legal entity | Not a separate legal entity |
| Liability | Limited to agreed contribution, except fraud | Unlimited, joint and several |
| Registration | Compulsory | Optional (section 69 disabilities) |
| Agency | Partner is agent of LLP only | Partner is agent of firm and other partners |
| Succession | Perpetual | Affected by death or insolvency, subject to contract |
| Maximum partners | No limit | 50 (prescribed under the Companies Act, 2013) |
| Property | Owned by the LLP | Owned by partners jointly |
| Compliance | Annual return and statement of account and solvency | Minimal |

questions.prompt: P and Q were the only partners of PQ LLP. Q died on 1 April 2026. P continued the business alone and, on 15 November 2026, the LLP took a loan from a bank. The LLP defaults. The bank seeks to make P personally liable. Decide with reasons.
questions.answer:
- Provision: section 6 - every LLP must have at least two partners. If the number falls below two and the LLP carries on business for more than six months while so reduced, the person who is the only partner during the time beyond six months, and who knows that it carries on business with him alone, is liable personally for the obligations of the LLP incurred during that period.
- Facts: partners reduced to one on 1 April 2026; the six-month period ended on 30 September 2026. The loan was taken on 15 November 2026, after six months. P knew he was the sole partner.
- Conclusion: P is personally liable to the bank for the loan, along with the LLP. Obligations incurred before the six months expired are the LLP's alone.

questions.prompt: Explain the provisions relating to designated partners of an LLP.
questions.answer:
- Section 7: every LLP must have at least two designated partners who are individuals, and at least one must be resident in India (stayed in India for at least 120 days during the financial year).
- If all partners are bodies corporate, or some are individuals and some bodies corporate, at least two individuals who are partners, or nominees of body corporate partners, act as designated partners.
- Designated partners are named in the incorporation document or become so with the consent of partners as per the LLP agreement; every partner may be a designated partner if the agreement so provides.
- They must give prior consent and obtain an identification number as prescribed.
- Section 8: they are responsible for doing all acts required for compliance with the Act, including filing documents, returns and statements, and are liable to penalties imposed on the LLP for contravention.

chapters.title: The Companies Act, 2013: Basics
chapters.summary: Nature and kinds of companies, incorporation, MoA and AoA, the doctrines of ultra vires, constructive notice and indoor management, and lifting the corporate veil.
chapters.lawAsOf: Companies Act, 2013 as amended up to 2026

lesson.heading: Nature of a company
lesson.body:
Section 2(20): a company is a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 or any previous company law. It is an artificial person created by law.

Characteristics:

- **Separate legal entity**: distinct from its members. **Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd. (1897)**: Salomon sold his business to a company in which he held almost all shares and was also a secured creditor. On winding up, the House of Lords held that the company was a different person from Salomon, so he was entitled to be paid as a secured creditor ahead of unsecured creditors.
- **Limited liability**: members are liable only to the extent of unpaid amount on shares or the guarantee.
- **Perpetual succession**: members may come and go, the company continues.
- **Separate property**: company's property belongs to it, not to members.
- **Transferability of shares** (restricted in a private company).
- **Common seal**: optional since the 2015 amendment.
- **Capacity to sue and be sued** in its own name.

lesson.heading: Kinds of companies
lesson.body:
| Basis | Kind | Section |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Liability | Limited by shares | 2(22) |
| Liability | Limited by guarantee | 2(21) |
| Liability | Unlimited company | 2(92) |
| Members | Private company | 2(68) |
| Members | Public company | 2(71) |
| Members | One Person Company | 2(62) |
| Control | Holding and subsidiary | 2(46), 2(87) |
| Control | Associate company (significant influence: at least 20% of total voting power, or control of business decisions under an agreement) | 2(6) |
| Ownership | Government company (at least 51% of paid-up share capital held by Central / State Government(s)) | 2(45) |
| Others | Section 8 company (charitable objects, profits applied to objects, no dividend) | 8 |
| Others | Foreign company | 2(42) |
| Others | Listed company | 2(52) |
| Others | Small company (paid-up capital and turnover within prescribed limits; not public, section 8 or holding / subsidiary) | 2(85) |
| Others | Dormant company | 455 |

**Private company** (section 2(68)): by its articles (i) restricts the right to transfer shares, (ii) limits members to **200** (except an OPC), excluding present and former employee-members, and joint holders counted as one, and (iii) prohibits invitation to the public to subscribe for securities.

**Public company** (section 2(71)): not a private company. A **subsidiary of a public company** is deemed public even if its articles say private.

Minimum members to form a company (section 3): **7** for public, **2** for private, **1** for OPC. Section 3A: if members fall below the minimum and the company carries on business for more than six months, every member aware of it is **severally liable** for debts contracted after those six months.

**OPC**: only a natural person who is an Indian citizen and resident in India may form it, and must name a nominee.

lesson.heading: Incorporation, MoA and AoA
lesson.body:
**Incorporation** (section 7): file with the Registrar the MoA and AoA signed by subscribers, a declaration of compliance by a professional engaged in formation or a director / manager / secretary, declarations by subscribers and first directors, address for correspondence, particulars of subscribers and first directors, and their consent. The Registrar issues a **certificate of incorporation** with a Corporate Identity Number (CIN). Section 7(7): if a company was incorporated by furnishing false information, the Tribunal may pass orders including making members' liability unlimited, removing the name, or winding up.

Section 9: from the date of incorporation the company is a body corporate with perpetual succession, capable of holding property, contracting and suing. Section 12: registered office within **30 days** of incorporation.

**Memorandum of Association** (section 4) is the charter; it defines the company's relation with outsiders. Clauses:

- **Name** clause: ending with 'Limited' (public) or 'Private Limited' (private).
- **Registered office** clause: the State.
- **Objects** clause.
- **Liability** clause.
- **Capital** clause (company with share capital).
- **Subscription / association** clause; for an OPC, the **nominee** clause.

Alteration: section 13, generally by special resolution, with approvals where required.

**Articles of Association** (section 5): rules for internal management; subordinate to the MoA and the Act (section 6 - the Act overrides MoA and AoA). Model forms are in Schedule I (Table F for a company limited by shares). Alteration by **special resolution** (section 14). **Entrenchment** provisions may require more restrictive procedures (section 5(3)). Section 10: MoA and AoA bind the company and members as if signed by each member.

lesson.heading: Doctrines: ultra vires, constructive notice, indoor management
Lifting the corporate veil
lesson.body:
The separate entity principle is the rule; courts and the Act disregard it in exceptional cases to look at the persons behind the company.

**Judicial grounds**:

- **Fraud or improper conduct**: **Gilford Motor Co. Ltd. v. Horne (1933)** - a former employee bound by a non-solicitation covenant formed a company to solicit customers; the court treated the company as a sham and granted an injunction against both.
- **Determining enemy character**: **Daimler Co. Ltd. v. Continental Tyre and Rubber Co. (1916)** - a company registered in England but controlled by Germans was treated as an enemy company.
- **Evasion of tax** or welfare legislation.
- **Sham or facade** company; company acting as agent of shareholders; protection of public policy.

**Statutory grounds** (Companies Act, 2013):

- section 3A: members severally liable when membership falls below the statutory minimum for over six months;
- section 7(7): incorporation by furnishing false information;
- sections 34 and 35: criminal and civil liability for untrue statements in a prospectus;
- section 339: fraudulent conduct of business discovered in winding up - persons responsible may be made personally liable without limit.

Exam tip: start every veil answer with Salomon's principle, then give judicial and statutory exceptions with one case each.

keyPoints: Section 2(20) company; separate legal entity (Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd., 1897).
Private company 2(68): restricts transfer, maximum 200 members, no public invitation. Minimum members: public 7, private 2, OPC 1 (section 3).
MoA (section 4) clauses: name, registered office, objects, liability, capital, subscription; AoA (section 5); alteration of articles by special resolution (section 14).
Ultra vires the company = void, cannot be ratified (Ashbury Railway Carriage v. Riche).
Constructive notice protects the company; indoor management protects outsiders (Royal British Bank v. Turquand). Exceptions: knowledge, suspicion, forgery.
Veil lifted: fraud (Gilford Motor v. Horne), enemy character (Daimler v. Continental Tyre), tax evasion; statutory: sections 3A, 7(7), 34-35, 339.

questions.prompt: The case that firmly established that a company is a legal person separate from its members is:
options: Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. v. Riche
Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.
questions.explanation: Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd. (1897): even a company dominated by one person is a separate legal entity.

questions.prompt: The maximum number of members of a private company (other than an OPC), excluding employee-members, is:
questions.explanation: Section 2(68): the articles must limit members to 200, excluding present and former employees who are members; joint holders count as one.

questions.prompt: The minimum number of persons required to form a public company is:
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(a): seven or more persons for a public company; two for a private company; one for an OPC.

questions.prompt: A private company which is a subsidiary of a public company is treated as:
options: A private company for all purposes
questions.explanation: Proviso to section 2(71): a subsidiary of a public company is deemed public even if its articles retain private company restrictions.

questions.prompt: A company in which not less than 51% of the paid-up share capital is held by the Central Government, or a State Government, or both, is a:
questions.explanation: Section 2(45) defines a Government company, including its subsidiaries.

questions.prompt: Articles of a company may be altered by:
questions.explanation: Section 14: subject to the Act and the MoA, articles are altered by special resolution. Conversion of a public into a private company also needs Tribunal approval.

questions.prompt: The doctrine of indoor management was laid down in:
options: Daimler Co. v. Continental Tyre and Rubber Co.
questions.explanation: Royal British Bank v. Turquand (1856): outsiders may assume internal formalities have been complied with.

questions.prompt: A company was held to be an enemy company because the persons in control of it were enemy aliens. The court lifted the veil in:
options: Daimler Co. v. Continental Tyre and Rubber Co.
questions.explanation: Daimler Co. Ltd. v. Continental Tyre and Rubber Co. (1916): veil lifted to determine enemy character.

questions.prompt: An act which is ultra vires the memorandum of a company can be ratified by a unanimous resolution of all its members.
questions.explanation: Ashbury Railway Carriage v. Riche: an act ultra vires the company is void ab initio and cannot be ratified even by all members.

questions.prompt: The doctrine of indoor management cannot be invoked by a person who relies on a forged document.
questions.explanation: Forgery is an exception; a forged document is a nullity and cannot bind the company.

questions.prompt: Which of these are clauses of the Memorandum of Association under section 4?
options: Clause on the quorum for Board meetings
questions.explanation: Section 4 requires name, registered office, objects, liability, capital (where applicable) and subscription clauses. Internal rules like quorum belong in the articles.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: A company must have a registered office capable of receiving communications within ___ days of its incorporation (section 12).
questions.explanation: Section 12(1): within 30 days of incorporation and at all times thereafter.

questions.prompt: Explain the doctrine of indoor management and its exceptions. How does it relate to the doctrine of constructive notice?
questions.answer:
- **Constructive notice**: MoA and AoA are public documents; every outsider is deemed to know their contents. It protects the company against outsiders.
- **Indoor management** (Royal British Bank v. Turquand, 1856): an outsider dealing in good faith may assume that internal requirements (meetings, quorum, resolutions) have been complied with. It protects outsiders and limits constructive notice: outsiders are deemed to know the documents but not whether internal procedures were followed. Section 176 gives a related statutory protection for acts of directors with defective appointments.
- **Exceptions**: (1) actual or constructive knowledge of the irregularity; (2) suspicion or negligence - circumstances calling for enquiry; (3) forgery - a forged document is a nullity; (4) acts beyond the apparent authority of the officer; (5) insiders such as directors cannot claim it.

questions.prompt: What is meant by lifting the corporate veil? State the circumstances in which the veil may be lifted.
questions.answer:
- Rule: a company is a separate legal entity (Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd.). Lifting the veil means disregarding this to identify the persons behind the company and hold them liable.
- Judicial grounds: fraud or improper conduct (Gilford Motor Co. v. Horne - company formed to evade a restrictive covenant); determination of enemy character (Daimler Co. v. Continental Tyre); evasion of tax; sham or facade company; company acting as agent of its members; protection of public policy.
- Statutory grounds under the Companies Act, 2013: section 3A (members below minimum for over six months - members aware are severally liable); section 7(7) (incorporation by false information); sections 34-35 (misstatement in prospectus); section 339 (fraudulent conduct of business in winding up - unlimited personal liability).

questions.prompt: The articles of Sunrise Ltd. allow directors to borrow up to any amount if authorised by an ordinary resolution of the general meeting. The directors borrowed ₹2 crore from Prakash without any such resolution. Prakash did not know of the omission. Sunrise Ltd. refuses to repay, claiming Prakash had constructive notice of the articles. Decide with reasons.
questions.answer:
- Provision: constructive notice deems Prakash to know the articles, so he is taken to know that a resolution was needed. The doctrine of indoor management (Royal British Bank v. Turquand) allows an outsider acting in good faith to assume that the internal requirement - passing the resolution - was complied with.
- Facts: the power to borrow existed under the articles subject to an internal procedure. Prakash had no knowledge of the omission and nothing suggests suspicion or forgery.
- Analysis: the case is on all fours with Turquand. Whether a general meeting passed a resolution is an internal matter Prakash could not verify.
- Conclusion: Sunrise Ltd. is bound and must repay Prakash. Its plea of constructive notice fails.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the Memorandum of Association and the Articles of Association.
questions.answer:
| Basis | Memorandum (section 4) | Articles (section 5) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | Charter of the company; defines its objects and powers | Rules for internal management |
| Relationship | Company with outsiders | Company with members, and among members |
| Status | Supreme document, subordinate only to the Act | Subordinate to the MoA and the Act (section 6) |
| Ultra vires acts | Acts beyond MoA are void and cannot be ratified | Acts beyond AoA but within MoA can be ratified by members |
| Alteration | Section 13, special resolution and approvals where required (e.g. change of State) | Section 14, special resolution |
| Model form | Schedule I, Tables A to E | Schedule I, Tables F to J |

chapters.title: The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
chapters.summary: Promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques, holder in due course, negotiation, crossing, presumptions and dishonour of cheques under section 138.
chapters.lawAsOf: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 as amended up to 2026

lesson.heading: Negotiable instruments and their kinds
lesson.body:
Section 13: a negotiable instrument means a **promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque** payable either to order or to bearer. Features: freely transferable by delivery (bearer) or indorsement and delivery (order); the transferee for value in good faith (holder in due course) gets a title free from defects of prior parties; the holder can sue in his own name; presumptions under section 118 apply.

| Basis | Promissory note (section 4) | Bill of exchange (section 5) | Cheque (section 6) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | Unconditional **undertaking** to pay | Unconditional **order** to pay | Bill drawn on a **specified banker**, payable on demand |
| Parties | Maker, payee | Drawer, drawee, payee | Drawer, drawee bank, payee |
| Acceptance | Not needed | Needed (unless payable on demand) | Not needed |
| Payable to bearer | Not allowed (section 31, RBI Act, 1934), except RBI / Government | Allowed, except on demand | Allowed |
| Days of grace | 3 days if not on demand | 3 days if not on demand | None |

Essentials of a promissory note: in writing; express promise to pay; unconditional; signed by the maker; certain maker and payee; certain sum of **money only**; stamped as required. A bank note or currency note is not a promissory note.

Section 6 includes the **electronic image of a truncated cheque** and a **cheque in electronic form**.

Section 18: if the amount in words and figures differs, the amount in **words** is payable. Section 17: an ambiguous instrument may be treated by the holder as either a note or a bill.

lesson.heading: Holder, holder in due course and negotiation
lesson.body:
**Holder** (section 8): a person entitled in his own name to possession and to receive the amount.

**Holder in due course** (section 9): a person who, **for consideration**, became the possessor (bearer instrument) or payee / indorsee (order instrument) **before the amount became payable**, without having sufficient cause to believe that any defect existed in the title of the person from whom he derived his title.

Privileges of an HDC: gets a good title even if a prior party's title was defective (section 58 does not bar him); prior parties are liable to him until the instrument is satisfied (section 36); estoppel against denying original validity (section 120) and the payee's capacity to indorse (section 121); a holder deriving title from an HDC has his rights, unless party to the fraud (section 53).

**Negotiation** (section 14): transfer making the transferee the holder. Bearer instrument - by delivery (section 47); order instrument - by **indorsement and delivery** (section 48).

Kinds of indorsement: **blank** (only signature; converts to bearer), **full / special** (names the indorsee), **restrictive** (stops further negotiation), **partial** (part of amount - not valid as negotiation, section 56), **conditional**, **sans recourse** (indorser excludes his liability), **facultative** (waives a right, e.g. notice of dishonour).

**Capacity** (section 26): every person competent to contract may bind himself. A **minor** may draw, indorse, deliver and negotiate so as to bind all parties **except himself**.

**Material alteration** (section 87) without the consent of the parties makes the instrument void against any party who did not consent, unless made to carry out the common intention of the original parties. Filling a blank in an inchoate instrument (section 20) or converting a blank indorsement into full are permitted.

lesson.heading: Crossing and presumptions
lesson.body:
**Crossing** is a direction to the drawee bank to pay only through a banker.

- **General crossing** (section 123): two parallel transverse lines, with or without words like 'and company' or 'not negotiable'. Payable only through a banker.
- **Special crossing** (section 124): the name of a banker added; payable only to that banker or its agent for collection.
- **'Not negotiable'** (section 130): the cheque remains transferable, but the transferee gets no better title than the transferor.
- **Account payee**: not defined in the Act; a banking-practice direction to the collecting banker to credit only the payee's account.
- A crossing may be made by the drawer or the holder (section 125).

**Presumptions** (section 118), until the contrary is proved: consideration; date; time of acceptance (within reasonable time after date and before maturity); time of transfer (before maturity); order of indorsements (as they appear); stamp; holder is a **holder in due course**. Section 139 adds a presumption that the holder of a cheque received it for discharge of a debt or liability.

lesson.heading: Dishonour of cheque: section 138
Common mistakes
lesson.body:
- Writing that a promissory note can be payable to bearer. Section 31 of the RBI Act prohibits it for anyone other than RBI or the Central Government (for demand notes).
- Mixing the 30-day notice period with the 15-day payment period.
- Treating a cheque for a gift or for a time-barred debt as covered by section 138. It covers only legally enforceable debts.
- Saying 'not negotiable' stops transfer. It does not; it only removes the holder in due course protection.
- Forgetting that a minor indorser binds all parties except himself.

keyPoints: Section 13: PN (section 4), bill of exchange (section 5), cheque (section 6) payable to order or bearer.
Holder in due course (section 9): for consideration, before maturity, in good faith without cause to suspect defect.
Section 118 presumptions; section 139 presumption for cheques; amount in words prevails (section 18).
Crossing: general (123), special (124), not negotiable (130).
Section 138: present within 6 months or validity; notice within 30 days of bank memo; 15 days to pay; complaint within 1 month (section 142).
Punishment: up to 2 years, or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both; interim compensation up to 20% (section 143A).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a negotiable instrument under section 13 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881?
questions.explanation: Section 13 names promissory notes, bills of exchange and cheques. Section 4 expressly excludes bank notes and currency notes from being promissory notes.

questions.prompt: 'I promise to pay Ramesh ₹50,000 after my marriage with Sita.' This instrument is:
options: Not a promissory note, as the promise is conditional
questions.explanation: A promissory note requires an unconditional undertaking. Marriage with a particular person is an uncertain event, so the promise is conditional.

questions.prompt: When the amount on a negotiable instrument is stated differently in words and figures, the amount payable is:
questions.explanation: Section 18: the amount stated in words is the amount undertaken or ordered to be paid.

questions.prompt: A cheque bearing two parallel transverse lines with the name 'State Bank of India' written between them is:
questions.explanation: Section 124: a cheque bearing the name of a banker is specially crossed to that banker; the transverse lines are not essential.

questions.prompt: Under section 138, the payee must give written notice to the drawer demanding payment within how many days of receiving information of dishonour from the bank?
questions.explanation: Proviso (b) to section 138: notice within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour. The drawer then has 15 days from receipt of notice to pay.

questions.prompt: An indorsement where the indorser writes 'without recourse to me' is called:
questions.explanation: A sans recourse indorsement excludes the indorser's liability to subsequent parties (section 52).

questions.prompt: A minor indorses a bill of exchange to Kunal. On dishonour, Kunal can hold liable:
questions.explanation: Section 26: a minor may draw, indorse, deliver and negotiate an instrument so as to bind all parties except himself.

questions.prompt: Writing the words 'not negotiable' on a crossed cheque makes it non-transferable.
questions.explanation: Section 130: the cheque remains transferable, but a transferee cannot get a better title than the transferor had.

questions.prompt: A cheque issued as a gift, which is dishonoured for insufficient funds, attracts an offence under section 138.
questions.explanation: Section 138 applies only to cheques issued for discharge of a legally enforceable debt or other liability. A gift is not a debt.

questions.prompt: Which presumptions apply under section 118 until the contrary is proved?
options: The instrument was made for consideration
The holder is a holder in due course
The drawer had sufficient funds in the account
questions.explanation: Section 118 presumes consideration, date, time of acceptance, transfer before maturity, order of indorsements, stamping and that the holder is a holder in due course. There is no presumption about funds.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: A person who, for consideration, became the holder of an instrument before maturity, without sufficient cause to believe any defect in the transferor's title, is a holder in ___ ___.
questions.explanation: Section 9 defines holder in due course.

questions.prompt: Vivek's cheque of ₹3,40,000, issued to repay a loan, was dishonoured for insufficient funds. All conditions of section 138 are met. What is the maximum fine the court can impose under section 138? Answer in ₹.
questions.explanation:
Section 138: fine may extend to twice the amount of the cheque.

| Particulars | Amount (₹) |
| --- | --- |
| Cheque amount | 3,40,000 |
| x 2 | |
| **Maximum fine** | **6,80,000** |

The court may also impose imprisonment up to two years, or both.

questions.prompt: Who is a holder in due course? Explain the privileges available to him.
questions.answer:
- Section 9: a person who, for consideration, became the possessor of a bearer instrument, or the payee or indorsee of an order instrument, before the amount became payable, without sufficient cause to believe that any defect existed in the title of the person from whom he derived title.
- Privileges:
- Gets a good title free from defects of prior parties (e.g. instrument obtained by fraud from an earlier holder).
- Every prior party is liable to him until the instrument is duly satisfied (section 36).
- Estoppel: maker, drawer and acceptor cannot deny the original validity of the instrument (section 120); maker and acceptor cannot deny the payee's capacity to indorse (section 121); indorser cannot deny prior signatures (section 122).
- An inchoate stamped instrument binds the signer to an HDC for any amount within the stamp (section 20).
- Presumption that every holder is an HDC (section 118(g)).
- A holder taking from an HDC gets his rights unless party to fraud (section 53).

questions.prompt: Nikhil issued a cheque dated 5 January 2027 for ₹2,00,000 to Sapna to repay a loan. Sapna presented it on 20 February 2027; it was returned for insufficient funds and she received the bank memo on 22 February 2027. She sent a notice on 30 March 2027, received by Nikhil on 2 April 2027. Nikhil did not pay. Can Sapna successfully prosecute Nikhil under section 138? Decide with reasons.
questions.answer:
- Provision: section 138 requires (a) a cheque for a legally enforceable debt, (b) presentment within its validity, (c) dishonour for insufficient funds, (d) written notice within **30 days** of receipt of the bank's information, and (e) failure to pay within 15 days of receipt of notice.
- Facts: the cheque was for a loan and was presented within validity; dishonour memo received 22 February 2027. The 30-day notice period ended on 24 March 2027. Notice was sent on 30 March 2027, after the deadline.
- Analysis: the notice requirement is mandatory. A late notice means the cause of action under section 138 does not arise on this dishonour.
- Conclusion: Sapna cannot prosecute Nikhil under section 138 on this dishonour. She may still file a civil suit to recover the ₹2,00,000 loan.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a bill of exchange and a cheque.
questions.answer:
| Basis | Bill of exchange (section 5) | Cheque (section 6) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drawee | Any person, including a banker | Always a specified banker |
| Payable | On demand or after a fixed period | Always on demand (subject to electronic forms) |
| Acceptance | Required if not payable on demand | Not required |
| Days of grace | 3 days, if not payable on demand | None |
| Crossing | Cannot be crossed | Can be crossed (sections 123-131) |
| Stopping payment | Not possible once accepted | Drawer can countermand before payment |
| Section 138 | Not applicable | Criminal liability on dishonour for insufficiency |
